name: Young blood transfusion

card.summary: Infusing plasma from young donors into older people, pursued by some as an anti-aging approach aimed at a younger-looking, better-functioning body.
card.aka: young plasma infusion, plasma transfusion for anti-aging
card.note: The US FDA has cautioned against commercial young-plasma treatments.

quick.overview:
Young blood transfusion means giving older people plasma donated by young people, in the hope of reversing age-related decline. The appearance idea is that a more youthful systemic environment could keep tissues, including skin and muscle, looking and behaving younger.

The concept comes from parabiosis experiments in which an old mouse shares circulation with a young one. In those animal studies, old tissues such as muscle and liver regenerated better. Human work has been small, mainly early trials in Alzheimer's disease, and has focused on safety and biomarkers rather than appearance.
quick.how: In clinics it has been offered as plasma infusions given as a medical procedure; the research protocols used short courses of weekly infusions. Some researchers are instead looking for individual circulating proteins, such as platelet factor 4, that may carry the effect.
quick.risks: As with any transfusion, risks include allergic reactions and volume overload. The FDA has warned consumers about commercial young-plasma offerings, citing lack of proven benefit.

lead: Young blood transfusion, also called young plasma infusion, is the transfer of plasma from young donors to older recipients to test or pursue systemic rejuvenation. It derives from heterochronic parabiosis, in which the circulations of a young and an old animal are surgically joined. [1]

For appearance, the proposed chain runs through general tissue renewal: if blood-borne factors from youth improve repair in muscle, liver, brain and other organs, the person might look and function younger. Animal studies report improvements in these tissues, but the evidence on visible aging in humans is not established. [2][1]

The modern wave began with a 2005 Stanford study by Irina Conboy and colleagues in which exposure to young mice restored regeneration of old muscle and liver. [1] Researchers have since pursued specific factors; a 2025 review describes platelet factor 4 as an element behind cognitive benefits seen with young blood. [3]

chain: Circulating factors alter aged tissue signalling
angle.text: Advocates frame it as renewing the body from the inside so skin, muscle and energy look and feel younger. The supporting evidence is from animal pairing studies and small human safety trials.

infobox: FDA has warned consumers about commercial offerings

paras: Parabiosis was developed by French physiologist Paul Bert in the 1860s, and Sauerbruch and Heyde produced long-term pairings in dogs in 1908. Mid-century gerontologists such as Clive McCay paired old and young rats. [1][2]

In the 2000s and 2010s, researchers reported that young blood improved neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity in aged mice (2011) and reversed demyelination (2012). Young mice exposed to old blood often showed signs of accelerated aging. [2]
Early human trials infused young donor plasma into people with mild Alzheimer's disease over short courses and found it tolerable, with modest, non-definitive changes in cognitive biomarkers. [1]

Grokipedia reports that the FDA has cautioned against commercial young-plasma treatments, citing insufficient proof of efficacy and risks of transfusion-related adverse events such as allergic reactions and volume overload, and that for-profit clinics were shut down. [1]

Researchers are trying to identify specific rejuvenating proteins or to dilute inhibitory factors in old plasma rather than transfuse whole plasma. A 2025 review discusses platelet factor 4 as needed for the cognitive benefits of young blood, the longevity factor klotho and exercise. [3][1]

Small early trials in Alzheimer's disease reported tolerability and modest biomarker changes; none has tested visible skin or physical appearance outcomes. [1] Most supportive findings come from mouse parabiosis experiments. [2]

timeline.event: Paul Bert's parabiosis experiments in rats. [1]
Sauerbruch and Heyde achieve long-term parabiotic dogs. [1]
Conboy et al. show young circulation restores old muscle and liver regeneration in mice. [1]
Villeda et al. report improved neurogenesis in aged mice. [2]
